name: Sodium bicarbonate
high_alert_note: Not confirmed as high-alert on a source read; the institution's list governs.
summary: Intravenous alkalinising agent for metabolic acidosis in conditions such as severe renal disease, uncontrolled diabetes, circulatory insufficiency due to shock and severe dehydration. Nursing focus: sodium and fluid overload, alkalosis and extravasation.
evidence_type_note: The evidence here is a regulator product label (prescribing information written for prescribers and pharmacists). It is not a bedside nursing practice guideline: the nursing actions are inferences from label warnings, marked partial, and the unit's protocol governs practice. Selected clinical evidence supplements the regulator label; full guideline and independent clinical appraisal remain outstanding.
jurisdiction_note: US FDA label only. EMA, MHRA and SFDA labels were not read; indications, warnings and presentations differ by country and by manufacturer.

items.text: The label indicates sodium bicarbonate injection in the treatment of metabolic acidosis that may occur in severe renal disease, uncontrolled diabetes, circulatory insufficiency due to shock or severe dehydration and similar states.

SSC 2026 advises against bicarbonate solely to improve circulation or reduce vasopressor needs in hypoperfusion-related lactic acidemia. Selected adults with septic shock, severe metabolic acidemia and moderate or severe AKI have a separate conditional recommendation with very low certainty.

BICARICU-2 found no significant improvement in mortality at 90 days, although kidney replacement therapy occurred less often. A 2026 pooled analysis likewise found no overall survival benefit; a signal in profound acidemia needs cautious interpretation. Do not equate correction of laboratory pH with improved survival.
Check the infusion site for extravasation and report any leakage promptly.
Monitoring frequency and alarm limits follow the unit's protocol for this medicine.

The label warns that solutions containing sodium ions should be used with great care, if at all, in patients with congestive heart failure, severe renal insufficiency, or other states with oedema and sodium retention, since intravenous administration can cause fluid or solute overload, lower serum electrolyte concentrations, overhydration or pulmonary oedema; extravascular infiltration should also be avoided.

The registered label identifies hazards when sodium bicarbonate is combined with norepinephrine, dobutamine or calcium-containing solutions. Request pharmacist assessment of the prescribed products and access plan before administration; do not improvise shared-line use or interrupt essential vasoactive support.

The registered label describes worsening alkalosis with potassium depletion and spasm associated with low calcium as pH rises. Reassess clinical findings and ordered laboratory results; seek clinician review for suspected overcorrection.
Solutions containing sodium should be used with great care, if at all, in congestive heart failure, severe renal insufficiency and oedematous states with sodium retention.
Intravenous administration can cause fluid or solute overload, overhydration, congestion or pulmonary oedema.

Routine bicarbonate is not recommended in adult cardiac arrest by AHA 2025 or as routine acute hyperkalaemia treatment by UKKA 2026. Special-circumstance treatment is a separate clinician-directed decision.

This registered injection is contraindicated in chloride loss from vomiting or continuous gastrointestinal suction, and in patients receiving diuretics known to cause hypochloraemic alkalosis. Clarify the indication, acid-base findings and chloride losses with the treating clinician.
Overly aggressive therapy can cause metabolic alkalosis (muscular twitching, irritability, tetany) and hypernatraemia; inadvertent extravasation is also described.

Escalate for tetany, twitching, breathlessness, fluid overload, suspected extravasation or any concern about an unsafe shared-line plan; seek urgent help for instability. Follow pharmacy and local policy for access decisions.

Use the unit's early warning score (for example, the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2 track-and-trigger system) to standardise recognition of acute deterioration: a medium aggregate score is a key trigger for an urgent clinical review, and a high aggregate score triggers an emergency clinical response. This is a generic nursing escalation framework, not specific to this medicine; it does not replace this medicine's own escalation triggers, which remain local protocol.
Record the product and order checks, monitoring results, adverse events and escalation per unit standard.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Inspect the infusion site for extravasation.
Watch for breathlessness, oedema and signs of fluid overload.
Review acid-base, sodium and potassium results as ordered.
Report tetany, twitching or fluid overload promptly.
Review other IV medicines and the planned access with pharmacy, particularly norepinephrine, dobutamine and calcium-containing products; report visible precipitate or cloudiness.

Review ordered acid-base and electrolyte results, including calcium when indicated; report new alkalosis, muscle twitching or tetany. Check sodium, urine output and fluid balance in patients at risk of sodium retention.
Assess ordered blood gas and electrolyte trends, ventilation, sodium and fluid balance; escalate worsening acidemia, respiratory compromise, suspected alkalosis or tissue injury.
Review chloride losses, gastrointestinal suction, relevant diuretics and ordered acid-base results before use; clarify suspected hypochloraemic alkalosis.
